chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Abdullah ibn Yahya al-Kahili, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

A man of impaired vision asked him (peace be upon him), and I was present, so he said, 'Can I apply Kohl when I enter the state of Ihram?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'No.' And why would you apply Kohl? He said, 'I am of impaired vision. So when I apply Kohl, it benefits me, and when I do not apply Kohl, it harms me.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'So apply Kohl.'

He said, 'Suppose I place something else along with the Kohl?' He (peace be upon him) said, 'What is it?' He said, 'I take two rags, fold them into squares, place one rag over each eye, and bind them with a strip to the back of my head. So when I do that, it benefits me, and when I neglect it, it harms me.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'So do it.'

key_terms.إِحْرَام: Ihram: The state of ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah
key_terms.ضَرَّنِي: Darrani: It harms me (indicating the consequence of omission)
key_terms.ضَرِيرُ الْبَصَر: Darir al-basar: One with impaired vision or blindness
key_terms.كُحْل: Kohl: A traditional eye cosmetic or medicinal powder applied to the eyes

ai.seo_question: Can a pilgrim in Ihram apply Kohl or cover their eyes if they have impaired vision?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi illustrates the Shia juristic principle of 'darurah' (necessity) overriding the general prohibition of covering the head and face in Ihram, specifically for medical treatment. The Imam’s concise ruling ('Do it') validates both the application of Kohl and the use of eye coverings as functional necessities rather than mere adornment, establishing a precedent for flexibility in ritual purity when health is at stake. This reflects the broader Shia emphasis on the removal of hardship (raf' al-haraj) in Islamic law.
